summary: A Chinese noun cannot follow a number or 这 / 那 directly: a measure word (classifier) comes in between — 一本书 ‘a book’, 这张桌子 ‘this table’, 那位老师 ‘that teacher’. The measure word is chosen by the kind or shape of the thing: 本 for bound books, 张 for flat things, 把 for things with a handle. 个 is the general one, used for people and for many things without a special measure word. Learn every noun with its measure word.

blocks.title: Like a German article
blocks.text: Learn 书 as ‘本 书’ just as you learn ‘das Buch’: the measure word is part of knowing the noun.

blocks.title: No measure word after 这些 / 那些, and none when 这 is alone
blocks.text: 这些书, 那些人 — and 这是书 ‘this is a book’.

blocks.title: 个 when in doubt
blocks.text: In speech 个 is heard with almost anything and is always understood; the specific measure word is what educated speech and writing expect.

items.title: 杯子 bēizi — the cup (a noun)
杯 bēi — a cup of (a measure)
points: 一杯水 a glass of water
一杯茶 a cup of tea

askYourself: Is there a number, 这 / 那 or 哪 before the noun? → it needs a measure word.
Is it a person? → 个, politely 位.
Is it a book? → 本. Flat (table, bed, paper)? → 张. Held by a handle (chair, key)? → 把. Long and thin (pen)? → 支.
A door or window? → 扇. A wall? → 面. A room? → 间. A building? → 栋. A lamp? → 盏. A phone? → 部.
Do I mean ‘a cup OF something’? → 杯; the cup itself → 一个杯子.
Is it 这些 / 那些, or 这 / 那 alone as the subject? → no measure word.
steps: Find the noun and recall its measure word.
Number / 这 / 那 + measure word + noun.
When you do not know it, 个 is understood — then learn the right one.

traps: *一书 / *这书 → 一本书, 这本书.
一个老师 and 一位老师 are both fine, but *一位人 is not: 位 goes with titles and respected people, not with 人 itself.
杯 vs 杯子: 一杯 is ‘a cup of’, 一个杯子 is ‘a cup’.
一 changes tone: yí ge, yí shàn, but yì běn, yì zhāng, yì bǎ.

quiz.why: Things with a flat top take 张.
Things held by a handle take 把.
位 is the polite measure word for people.
No measure word after 这些.

seeAlso.note: German counts mass nouns with measure nouns — ein Blatt Papier (一张纸), eine Tasse Kaffee (一杯咖啡), zwei Stück Kuchen; Chinese needs one with every counted noun.
Arabic has no measure words; the difficulty is elsewhere — the number agrees with the noun (gender polarity for 3–10).
Hebrew has no measure words; numbers have masculine and feminine forms chosen by the noun’s gender.
